**Verdict:** True; no flaw found.

**Theorem.** For $n\ge2$, let $P(x)=x_0\oplus\cdots\oplus x_{n-1}$ and $\mathcal C=\{x_i\}\cup\{\neg(x_i\land x_j):i,j\}$ (so $\neg x_i\in\mathcal C$). Let $m(n)$ be the least $|S|$, $S\subseteq\{0,1\}^n$, such that every $f\in\mathcal C$ disagrees with $P$ somewhere on $S$. Then $m(n)=2$ for $n$ even and $m(n)=3$ for $n$ odd.

**Proof.** One point never suffices: if $S=\{u\}$ and $p=P(u)$, then for any $i$, either $x_i(u)=p$ or $\neg x_i(u)=p$; that member of $\mathcal C$ is not distinguished.

Let $n$ be odd and $S=\{u,v\}$, with $p=P(u)$, $q=P(v)$. Distinguishing both $x_i$ and $\neg x_i$ requires $(x_i(u),x_i(v))\notin\{(p,q),(\neg p,\neg q)\}$ for every $i$. If $p=q$, the remaining columns are $(0,1),(1,0)$, so $v=\bar u$; but for odd $n$, $P(\bar u)=\neg P(u)$, contradicting $p=q$. If $p\ne q$, the remaining columns are $(0,0),(1,1)$, so $u=v$, contradicting $p\ne q$. Thus $m(n)\ge3$.

If $n$ is even, $S=\{0^n,1^n\}$ works: $P=0$ at both points; every NAND, including $\neg x_i$, equals $1$ at $0^n$, and every $x_i$ equals $1$ at $1^n$. Hence $m(n)=2$.

If $n$ is odd, take $0^n$, all-ones except bit $0$ is $0$, and all-ones except bit $1$ is $0$. Each has $P=0$, since $n-1$ is even. Every NAND equals $1$ at $0^n$; every $x_i$ equals $1$ at one of the other two points. Hence $m(n)\le3$, so $m(n)=3$. ∎

This is only a finite distinguishing-set statement; it implies no asymptotic complexity separation.
